relationship: later identification and citation of the prophet
rationale: Micah's opening places Michaiah of Morashthi in Hezekiah's reign. Jeremiah identifies Micah the Morathite in that reign and cites the warning found in Micah 3:12. The reign and cited warning support the connection while the supplied name forms remain unchanged.

relationship: earth summoned before divine testimony and judgment
rationale: Micah summons the peoples and earth to attend to the Lord's testimony from His holy house. The psalm likewise summons the earth, presents God's manifestation from Zion and calls heaven and earth to His judgment.

relationship: judgment proceeding from God's dwelling to the earth
rationale: Micah depicts the Lord coming out of His place and descending upon the earth's heights. Isaiah announces the Lord bringing wrath from the holy place upon earth's inhabitants; both move from God's dwelling to judgment on earth.

relationship: shaken earth and wax-melting imagery
rationale: Micah's mountains are shaken and its valleys melt like wax before fire. The psalm likewise describes the shaken earth, with mountains melting like wax before the Lord. The shared shaking and wax imagery preserve the different landscape features named as melting.

relationship: Samaria as a focus of Israel's religious offense
rationale: Micah identifies Samaria with Jacob's impiety. Hosea rebukes Samaria's calf, declares that a craftsman made it and it is no god, and speaks of God's anger. Both locate Israel's offense concretely in Samaria.

relationship: same-book parallel fates of the two capitals
rationale: Samaria is to become a fruit watcher's hut amid agricultural ground. The later warning similarly makes Jerusalem a fruit watcher's hut and Zion a plowed field, linking the two capitals named in the book's opening through parallel ruin imagery.

relationship: destruction of idolatrous objects
rationale: Micah announces the cutting up of Samaria's carved images and obliteration of her idols. Deuteronomy commands the burning of graven images. The shared connection is destruction of the images; Micah specifically assigns the wages to the fire.

relationship: lament associated with sirens
rationale: Micah compares the city's lament with dragons and daughters of sirens. Job calls himself a brother to sirens while describing crying out and song becoming weeping. Both associate lament with sirens, preserving their differing companion animal names.

relationship: narrative counterpart to a threat reaching Jerusalem
rationale: Micah says the blow reaches Judah and Jerusalem. Kings narrates the Assyrian capture of Judah's fortified cities and a great force sent onward to Jerusalem. The connection concerns that advance into Judah toward Jerusalem, without equating every detail of the oracle with the campaign.

relationship: Gath and rejoicing over Israel's calamity
rationale: Micah tells those in Gath not to magnify themselves in the midst of the lament. David likewise forbids reporting Israel's defeat in Gath lest foreign daughters rejoice. Both address Gath's possible exultation over Israel's misfortune.

relationship: parallel divine judgment against Jerusalem
rationale: Micah attributes the calamities at Jerusalem's gates to the Lord. Ezekiel explicitly identifies Jerusalem and declares that the Lord is against her and will execute judgment within her because His ordinances were rejected.

relationship: military connection between Lachish and Jerusalem
rationale: Micah addresses Lachish amid the noise of chariots and horsemen and relates her to Zion's trouble. Kings records an Assyrian force sent from Lachish against Jerusalem. Both passages connect the two cities in a military setting, without making the historical report explain every charge against Lachish.

relationship: hair cutting and mourning for loved ones
rationale: Micah commands shaving and shearing in mourning for children taken captive. Amos likewise joins baldness on every head with lamentation and mourning for a beloved one. The shared mourning signs are retained without changing Micah's separate widowhood-and-eagle wording.

relationship: evil planned upon a bed
rationale: Micah describes wrongdoers planning evil on their beds before carrying it out. The psalm likewise depicts the lawless person devising lawlessness upon his bed and refusing the good way.

relationship: parallel condemnation of land seizure
rationale: Micah condemns coveting fields and plundering a person, house and inheritance. Isaiah likewise condemns joining house to house and field to field in order to take from a neighbor.

relationship: narrative example of seized inheritance
rationale: Micah condemns taking a person's field and inheritance. Kings records Ahab going to possess Naboth's vineyard after Naboth's death, following the refusal to surrender his ancestral inheritance in the surrounding account.

relationship: parallel announcement of planned calamity
rationale: The Lord declares that He is planning calamities against the offending tribe. Jeremiah similarly announces the Lord's shaping evils and devising a design against Judah and Jerusalem, alongside a call to turn from evil practices.

relationship: shared loss through division of the people's land
rationale: Micah's lament says the people's portion was measured and their fields divided. Joel announces judgment over the nations concerning Israel's scattering and the division of the Lord's land. Both describe dispossession through division of the land.

relationship: loss contrasted with inheritance allotted by lot
rationale: Micah threatens the loss of anyone casting a measuring cord by lot in the Lord's assembly. Joshua's account surveys the land into portions and casts a lot before the Lord, providing the positive allotment practice with which Micah's exclusion contrasts.

relationship: provoking God's Spirit
rationale: Micah cites the claim that Jacob's house provoked the Lord's Spirit. Isaiah describes the people disobeying and provoking His holy spirit, followed by the Lord turning against them. The connection concerns the stated provocation, not an imported claim that God's patience is short.

relationship: same-book imagery of flaying the people
rationale: Micah 2 describes hostility through the image of flaying skin. Chapter 3 develops the charge against leaders with skins stripped from the people and their flesh treated as meat, repeating the book's bodily imagery of abuse.

relationship: luxury followed by captivity
rationale: Micah says the people's leaders will be expelled from luxurious houses because of their practices. Amos likewise describes powerful people reclining on ivory beds and enjoying costly food and perfume, then announces captivity.

relationship: uncleanness and loss of a place to remain
rationale: Micah commands departure because uncleanness has made the place no resting place. Leviticus connects defilement of the land with the Lord driving out its inhabitants and warns Israel against the same defilement.

relationship: shared pursuit-without-a-pursuer language
rationale: Micah describes being pursued with no one pursuing. Leviticus' covenant sanctions include fleeing when no one pursues, alongside defeat before enemies. The paradoxical pursuit language is the specific connection.

relationship: Israel's gathering portrayed as a flock
rationale: Micah promises to gather Israel's remaining ones, compares them with sheep in affliction and a flock within its resting place, and says they will leap out from among people. Ezekiel likewise uses flock language for gathering from countries, then explicitly promises pasture and rest.

relationship: shared flock leadership through an opening
rationale: Micah's gathered flock passes through a gate with its king before it and the Lord leading. John describes the opened sheepfold, the shepherd leading his sheep out and going before them. The connection is the shared leadership image, not a claim that the passages narrate the same event.

relationship: leaders' responsibility for justice
rationale: Micah asks Israel's authorities whether they ought to know justice. Deuteronomy directs appointed judges and officers to judge the people with righteous judgment, supplying the explicit responsibility challenged by the question.

relationship: opposition between corrupt preferences and the call to good
rationale: Micah accuses leaders of hating good and seeking evil. Amos calls for seeking good rather than evil and restoring judgment, directly opposing the preferences Micah condemns.

relationship: shared imagery of devouring the people
rationale: Micah describes the people's flesh treated as meat for a cooking pot. The psalm similarly accuses lawless people of devouring the people like a meal of bread. Both use eating imagery to portray abuse of the people.

relationship: violence followed by rejected prayer
rationale: Micah says the Lord will not hear the cry of those who acted wickedly against the people and will turn His face away. Isaiah likewise says He will turn His eyes away and refuse multiplied supplications because their hands are full of blood.

relationship: corrupt prophetic pronouncements tied to food
rationale: Micah's misleading prophets proclaim peace when their mouths are supplied and raise war when they are not. Ezekiel condemns profaning God through vain pronouncements for barley and scraps of bread; both connect deceptive prophetic activity with food received.

relationship: shared judgment imagery of lost daylight
rationale: Micah announces night in place of vision and sunset over the prophets. Amos similarly announces the sun setting at midday and light becoming dark during daytime. Micah applies the darkness specifically to the prophets' loss of vision.

relationship: prophets ashamed of their visions
rationale: Micah announces shame for dream-seers and mockery for diviners. Zechariah likewise says prophets will be ashamed because of their visions when they prophesy.

relationship: commission to declare Jacob's sins
rationale: Micah links strength in the Lord's Spirit with declaring Jacob's impieties and Israel's sins. Isaiah likewise commands a strong public proclamation of the people's sins and Jacob's lawless acts.

relationship: perverted justice opposed to the legal requirement
rationale: Micah charges leaders with abhorring justice and twisting what is straight. Deuteronomy forbids perverting judgment and commands pursuit of what is just, directly opposing that conduct.

relationship: parallel condemnation of building with bloodshed
rationale: Micah condemns building Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices. Habakkuk pronounces woe on building and preparing a city with bloodshed and injustices, repeating the distinctive city-building accusation.

relationship: judicial payment opposed to the ban on bribes
rationale: Micah accuses Jerusalem's leaders of judging for gifts. Deuteronomy explicitly forbids judges taking a bribe because it blinds the wise and overturns righteous words.

relationship: explicit later citation of Micah's warning
rationale: Jeremiah explicitly attributes to Micah the warning that Zion will be plowed as a field and the house's mountain become woodland. Those clauses correspond to this verse; Jeremiah's description of Jerusalem as an untrodden place is preserved alongside Micah's fruit watcher's hut wording.

relationship: parallel oracle of the elevated Lord's mountain
rationale: Both passages locate the vision in the last days, raise the Lord's mountain above surrounding heights and describe peoples or nations coming toward it.

relationship: parallel invitation to learn at Zion
rationale: Both passages have nations invite one another to the Lord's mountain and Jacob's God's house, to learn His way and walk in it. Both end with law going from Zion and the Lord's word from Jerusalem.

relationship: parallel transformation of weapons into tools
rationale: Both describe divine judgment among peoples followed by swords becoming plows and spears becoming sickles. Each concludes with nations no longer taking up war or learning to wage it.

relationship: contrasting prophetic uses of weapons and farming tools
rationale: Micah describes weapons remade into farming tools as war ends. Joel reverses that direction, ordering farming tools made into weapons while gathering nations for judgment. The same implements serve contrasting scenes in their respective oracles.

relationship: parallel vine-and-fig-tree peace imagery
rationale: Micah promises rest beneath each person's vine and fig tree without fear. Zechariah likewise pictures neighbors invited beneath a vine and fig tree in the promised day.

relationship: shared declaration of allegiance to the Lord
rationale: Micah contrasts the peoples' own ways with the community's lasting walk in the Lord's name. Joshua similarly contrasts available objects of service with his household's declared service of the Lord.

relationship: parallel gathering of the crushed and rejected
rationale: Micah promises to gather the crushed and receive the expelled. Zephaniah likewise promises gathering of the crushed and saving and receiving the oppressed and rejected.

relationship: the Lord's kingship associated with Mount Zion
rationale: Micah promises that the Lord will reign over the restored people on Mount Zion. Obadiah likewise joins people ascending from Mount Zion with the declaration that the kingdom will be the Lord's.

relationship: Zion's distress compared to labor pains
rationale: Micah asks why Zion has been seized with pains like a woman giving birth. Jeremiah likewise describes the daughter of Zion's voice and groaning as those of a woman in labor amid calamity.

relationship: rescue from Babylon
rationale: Micah announces that Zion will reach Babylon and that the Lord will redeem her there from enemies. Isaiah calls the people to leave Babylon and proclaim that the Lord rescued His servant Jacob.

relationship: hostile rejoicing over Judah's distress
rationale: Micah describes gathered nations declaring that they will rejoice over Zion. Obadiah explicitly forbids rejoicing and boasting over Judah's destruction and affliction, condemning the response Micah attributes to the hostile nations.

relationship: gathered nations compared to an agricultural judgment
rationale: Micah says the nations have been gathered like sheaves on a threshing floor despite not understanding God's counsel. Joel likewise gathers nations for judgment and depicts a ready vintage and full winepress. The agricultural forms differ, but both portray their gathering as preparation for judgment.

relationship: Israel equipped for threshing imagery of victory
rationale: Micah equips Zion with iron horns and bronze hooves to thresh and grind peoples. Isaiah makes Jacob like saw-toothed threshing wagon wheels that grind mountains and hills into dust. Both portray the people as divinely equipped threshing instruments.

relationship: shared image of humiliating blows to the cheeks
rationale: Micah announces that Israel's tribes will be struck on the cheek with a rod. Isaiah's speaker gives his cheeks to slaps and faces shameful spitting. The connection is the depicted facial humiliation; the passages' subjects are preserved as distinct.

relationship: explicit later use of the Bethlehem ruler oracle
rationale: Micah announces a ruler for Israel coming from Bethlehem. Matthew explicitly introduces a prophetic text naming Bethlehem as the ruler's birthplace in response to the question about the Christ. Matthew's by-no-means-least formulation remains distinct from Micah's smallness wording.

relationship: childbirth associated with a people's restoration
rationale: Micah connects the woman's giving birth with the remaining brothers' return to Israel. Isaiah connects Zion giving birth to her children with the birth of a nation. The shared childbirth-and-people imagery does not identify Micah's unnamed woman with a particular individual.

relationship: parallel shepherd-ruler promises
rationale: Micah's promised ruler will shepherd his flock in the Lord's strength. Ezekiel likewise promises one shepherd, God's servant David, and calls him a ruler among the people, joining shepherding with rule under the Lord.

relationship: parallel response to Assyrian intrusion
rationale: Micah describes an Assyrian entering the land and a response raised against him. Isaiah promises destruction of the Assyrians from the Lord's land and mountains. Both address Assyrian intrusion and its reversal; Micah's seven shepherds and eight bites wording is left intact.

relationship: parallel deliverance from Assyria's power
rationale: Micah promises rescue from Assour when he crosses the land's borders. Isaiah similarly announces removal of the Assyrians from the land and removal of their yoke.

relationship: dew imagery connected with Israel and the Lord
rationale: Micah compares Jacob's remnant among the peoples with dew falling from the Lord. Hosea promises that the Lord will be like dew to Israel. Both connect Israel and dew with the Lord, while assigning the image differently.

relationship: shared lion imagery with no rescuer
rationale: Micah depicts the remnant as a lion seizing among flocks with no one to deliver. Hosea likewise uses a lion comparison and seizure with no one to rescue. Micah applies the image to the remnant; Hosea applies it to the Lord's judgment against Judah.

relationship: hands over enemies as victory imagery
rationale: Micah promises the hand raised over afflicting enemies. Jacob's blessing of Judah likewise places his hands upon his enemies' backs, using the position of the hand to express victory over opponents.

relationship: parallel removal of horses and chariots
rationale: Micah announces destruction of the people's horses and chariots. Zechariah likewise announces the destruction of chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, placing that removal beside peace and the coming king's rule.

relationship: judgment on fortified cities
rationale: Micah promises to destroy cities and remove strongholds. Hosea specifically condemns Judah's multiplication of walled cities and announces fire that will devour their foundations.

relationship: removal of forbidden sorcery and divination
rationale: Micah announces removal of sorceries and utterers of oracles. Deuteronomy forbids sorcery, divination and related practices among Israel and contrasts the nations' reliance on them with the Lord's instruction.

relationship: parallel destruction of images and pillars
rationale: Micah promises destruction of carved images and pillars and an end to bowing to handmade works. Deuteronomy commands the breaking of pillars and burning of graven images, sharing the elimination of these objects of worship.

relationship: parallel cutting down of sacred groves
rationale: Micah promises to cut down the groves from the people's midst. Deuteronomy specifically commands cutting down sacred groves along with destroying other objects of foreign worship.

relationship: parallel wrath against nations
rationale: Micah announces vengeance in anger and wrath among disobedient nations. Isaiah summons nations to hear that the Lord's wrath and anger are against them for destruction, matching the announced agent, recipients and punitive anger.

relationship: creation summoned to hear the divine case
rationale: Micah calls for the mountains and hills to hear the word in the setting of judgment. Moses likewise calls heaven and earth to hear his words, using creation as the audience to a declaration concerning God and His people.

relationship: creation as witness to God's judgment of His people
rationale: Micah calls the hills, ravines and earth's foundations to hear the Lord's case with Israel. The psalm likewise summons heaven and earth to God's judgment of His covenant people and declares God the judge.

relationship: parallel divine question about an alleged offense
rationale: The Lord asks His people what He has done to grieve or trouble them. Jeremiah similarly asks what offense their fathers found in Him that led them away, framing the people's departure against God's challenge to name His wrongdoing.

relationship: explicit recollection of deliverance from slavery
rationale: Micah recalls the Lord bringing Israel from Egypt and redeeming them from the house of slavery. Exodus uses that same Egypt-and-house-of-bondage description in the Lord's declaration introducing the commandments.

relationship: explicit recollection of Balak and Balaam
rationale: Micah commands remembrance of Balak's plan and Balaam's answer. Numbers records Balak summoning Balaam to curse Jacob, Balaam's refusal to curse those God does not curse, and Balak's complaint that a blessing was given instead.

relationship: questioning the sufficiency of animal offerings
rationale: Micah asks whether burnt offerings and calves can be the means of taking hold of the Lord. The psalm likewise discusses continual burnt offerings, refuses calves and questions whether God eats bulls' flesh, directing attention beyond merely supplying sacrificial animals.

relationship: sacrificial abundance contrasted with obedience
rationale: Micah asks whether thousands of rams can satisfy the Lord before stating what He seeks in the next verse. Samuel explicitly places listening and obedience above sacrifice and the fat of rams.

relationship: firstborn sacrifice considered against the rejection of child offerings
rationale: Micah asks whether a firstborn child could be given for sin, followed by the Lord's ethical requirements. Deuteronomy explicitly rejects the nations' burning of sons and daughters as practices the Lord hates, bearing on the proposed child offering.

relationship: parallel statement of what the Lord requires
rationale: Micah asks what the Lord seeks and names justice, mercy and readiness to walk with Him. Deuteronomy likewise asks what He requires and names fear, walking in His ways, love, service and keeping His commands.

relationship: justice and mercy as weighty requirements
rationale: Micah identifies doing justice and loving mercy among what God seeks. Jesus likewise names justice and mercy among the Law's weightier matters, contrasting their neglect with meticulous tithing.

relationship: salvation promised to those who fear the Lord
rationale: Micah says the Lord will save those who fear His name. The psalm likewise says He hears and saves those who fear Him, directly joining reverence and rescue.

relationship: treasure and the lawless person
rationale: Micah exposes a lawless person's house storing lawless treasures. Proverbs warns that treasures do not profit lawless people and contrasts them with righteousness that rescues from death.

relationship: deceptive weights opposed to the legal standard
rationale: Micah questions whether a lawless person can be justified with deceptive weights in a pouch. Deuteronomy expressly forbids differing weights in the pouch, requires just weights and condemns the injustice.

relationship: wealth associated with deceit and impiety
rationale: Micah links accumulated wealth with impiety and the inhabitants' false speech. Jeremiah likewise describes houses filled with deceit whose owners became great and rich, followed by their failure to judge rightly and the promise of visitation.

relationship: punishment for sins preceding agricultural deprivation
rationale: Micah announces striking and obliteration because of sins, followed by hunger and crop losses. Leviticus similarly announces discipline for sins followed by ineffective labor and land and trees failing to yield.

relationship: shared curse of eating without satisfaction
rationale: Micah says the people will eat but not be filled. Leviticus uses the same eating-without-being-filled warning within the covenant's scarcity-of-bread sanctions.

relationship: parallel loss of grain, wine and olive yield
rationale: Micah announces sowing without reaping, pressing olives without anointing and pressing wine without drinking. Deuteronomy likewise warns of failed grain yield, vineyards whose wine is not drunk and olives that give no oil for anointing.

relationship: shared imagery of an absent fruit crop
rationale: Micah laments the lack of an available cluster at the vintage. Jeremiah likewise describes vines without grapes and fig trees without figs. Both portray fruitlessness in passages that also address the people's wrongdoing.

relationship: shared lament for vanished faithfulness
rationale: Micah laments that the devout person has perished and no one acts rightly among people. The psalm similarly cries that the holy one is gone and truths have diminished, followed by deceit toward neighbors.

relationship: shared moth-consumption imagery of loss
rationale: Micah pictures removal of the people's good things with a moth eating away. Isaiah likewise speaks of wool eaten by a moth, in contrast to God's lasting righteousness and salvation. The connection is the consuming-moth image; Micah's other wording remains unchanged.

relationship: parallel warning against trust in familiar companions
rationale: Micah warns against confidence in friends and even disclosure to a bed companion. Jeremiah likewise warns people to guard against neighbors and not trust brothers because friends act deceitfully.

relationship: explicitly corresponding household-division language
rationale: Micah lists son against father, daughter against mother, daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, and enemies within the household. Matthew reproduces the same family divisions and household-enemy statement in Jesus' description of division associated with His coming.

relationship: waiting for the Lord and being heard
rationale: The speaker in Micah resolves to wait upon God the Savior and expects Him to listen. The psalm recalls waiting patiently for the Lord and being heard, giving an answered-prayer counterpart to that expectation.

relationship: falling, rising and forbidden enemy rejoicing
rationale: The speaker in Micah tells the enemy not to rejoice at the speaker's fall because rising will follow. Proverbs likewise says the righteous fall and rise and then forbids rejoicing over an enemy's fall.

relationship: acknowledgment of sin amid divine displeasure
rationale: The speaker in Micah bears the Lord's anger because of acknowledged sin, while awaiting vindication. Lamentations similarly questions grumbling over one's sin, calls for return to the Lord and acknowledges godlessness and unappeased divine displeasure.

relationship: shared taunt about God's whereabouts
rationale: Micah records an enemy asking where the speaker's God is. The psalmist likewise hears the repeated taunt, Where is your God, while suffering in tears. Both place that question in the mouth of those aggravating the afflicted person's distress.

relationship: judgment according to the fruits of conduct
rationale: Micah attributes the land's obliteration to the fruits of its inhabitants' practices. Jeremiah states that the Lord gives to each according to their ways and the fruits of their practices, articulating the principle behind such recompense.

relationship: prayer to Israel's divine shepherd
rationale: Micah asks God to shepherd the people, described as the sheep of His inheritance. The psalm likewise addresses the One shepherding Israel and guiding Joseph like sheep, then asks Him to come and save.

relationship: explicit recollection of the exodus as a pattern of wonders
rationale: Micah promises wonders like those seen at the departure from Egypt. Exodus narrates the Lord rescuing Israel from the Egyptians and Israel seeing His great hand, providing the recalled deliverance pattern.

relationship: nations seeing and mouths falling silent
rationale: Micah depicts nations seeing God's work and putting hands over their mouths. Isaiah likewise depicts nations marveling and kings closing their mouths as they see what had not been proclaimed to them. Both portray a silenced response to what they witness, in differing prophetic settings.

relationship: shared serpent-and-earth humiliation imagery
rationale: Micah compares the nations licking dust with snakes moving along the ground. Genesis condemns the serpent to go on breast and belly and eat earth. The connection is the degrading serpent-and-earth image, not an identification of the nations with that individual serpent.

relationship: shared dust-licking image of humbled opponents
rationale: Micah depicts the nations licking dust and fearing God. The royal psalm likewise describes enemies licking dust, with kings bowing and nations serving, using the same action to express humbled opposition.

relationship: shared question of God's incomparability
rationale: Micah asks who is a God like the Lord in the context of mercy and forgiveness. The exodus song similarly asks who is like the Lord among the gods, praising His wondrous works. The shared rhetorical question introduces praise with different immediate emphases.

relationship: shared mercy and removal of wrongdoing
rationale: Micah praises God for removing injustices, passing over impieties and desiring mercy. Exodus's proclamation of His name likewise emphasizes mercy and the taking away of lawlessness, injustice and sins.

relationship: spatial imagery of sins removed from the people
rationale: Micah pictures injustices sunk and sins thrown into the sea's depths. The psalm describes lawless deeds removed as far as east from west. Both use distance or depth to portray God's removal of the people's wrongdoing.

relationship: appeal to the oath given to Abraham
rationale: Micah anticipates mercy to Abraham according to what God swore to the fathers. Genesis records the Lord swearing by Himself to bless Abraham's offspring and, through that offspring, the nations.

relationship: shared appeal to ancestral mercy and Abraham's oath
rationale: Micah joins mercy to Abraham with the oath sworn to the fathers. Luke's song likewise joins mercy to the fathers, remembrance of the holy covenant and the oath sworn to Abraham.
